source: nflverse data (play-by-play, FTN charting, PFR advanced stats, snap counts, rosters), CC BY 4.0. Calculations by Raiders Rundown.

qb.name: Passing value
qb.why: EPA per dropback (passes, sacks and scrambles) is the most reliable quarterback number and the best predictor of the next stretch; success rate, win probability added and mixes of them predict no better. It still carries his scheme, protection and receivers.

rb.name: Rushing components
rb.why: Rushing EPA and success rate barely repeat from one season to the next (r = .13), so no overall grade is defensible. Explosive-run rate and yards after contact are graded as separate components; they overlap (a back who breaks tackles also breaks long runs), so they are never averaged. Rushing yards over expected is tracking data that covers only some carries and repeats poorly (reliability about .26): it is shown as an observed number with the carries it covers, and is not graded.

wr.name: Receiving efficiency
wr.why: Success rate on targets is more reliable than EPA per target (a few long plays swing EPA) and predicts next season as well. It is efficiency, not role: targets and depth of target describe how he is used. Separation at the moment the pass arrives, measured only on his targets, describes how open the quarterback found him; it is not a measure of route running on every play, and it is shown apart and never graded.

te.name: Receiving efficiency
te.why: Same as receivers: success rate on targets, with role (targets, depth of target) and the tracking description of how open he was when targeted shown apart. Tight ends have few targets, so the interval is wide.

edge.name: Pass rush
edge.why: Pressure rate is both reliable and persistent for pass rushers; sacks are not, and tackling is a different trait.

lb.name: Production and role
lb.why: A linebacker's stable numbers are tackles and targets per snap, which are role (year to year r = .81). His coverage results do not repeat (r = .12). The public data does not say who he covered, so these are production and context, not a quality grade.

cb.name: Production and role
cb.why: Yards per target allowed does not repeat from one season to the next (r = .06) and the public data does not say who a corner covered. What follows is what happened when he was targeted, not a judgement of him.

saf.name: Production and role
saf.why: A safety's coverage results do not repeat from season to season (r = .05 to .13) and are shared with the coverage around him. These are production and context.

ol.name: Record
ol.why: The public data has no block won or lost for a single lineman. His line's numbers are shared by the five who start together.

k.name: Kicking components
k.why: Field goals made above what the distance predicts do not repeat from one season to the next (r is about zero), so they are shown as production and never graded. Kickoff value does repeat a little, and is graded as its own component.

p.name: Punting value
p.why: Expected points added per punt, with net yards as a second view. Both repeat modestly from season to season.

pr.name: Production
pr.why: A punt returner's value per return is almost all situation: the measured reliability of it across seasons is close to zero. Shown as production.

kr.name: Return value
kr.why: Expected points added per kickoff return, with average return yards as a second view.

pairwise.target: P(A's EPA per dropback in the games after the cutoff > B's in the same games), relative to the league in those games, counting the uncertainty in both estimated levels and the luck in both outcomes

display.rule: shown rounded DOWN to the step, never above the cap (the top bucket's realized rate, rounded down); below the floor the pair is too close to call; quarterback pairs only, both with 4 to 10 games
